issue: Register mismatch: 이분 (honorific 'this esteemed person') used to introduce one's OWN friend. Koreans elevate teachers/elders with 이분 but introduce friends/juniors with neutral 이쪽 (Sogang/Yonsei convention: 이쪽은 제 친구예요). Honoring your own friend to a third party sounds off.

fix.grammar: 이쪽 (ijjok = this side) politely introduces a friend or equal: 이쪽은 제 친구예요.

issue: Honorific inconsistency: subject is honored with 이분 AND is a teacher, yet the copula is plain 이에요. A Seoul speaker introducing 박 선생님 says 이세요 (subject-honorific -시- within 해요체, still -요 ending, present tense). NOTE: engine gap — haeyo('이시다') would derive 이셔요; '이시다': '이세요' must be added to IRREGULARS in src/data/conjugation/ko.ts.

fix.grammar: -세요 respects the person you talk about: 선생님이세요 (seonsaengnim-iseyo = is [my] teacher).

issue: Stiff phrasing: 직업이 뭐예요? is form-filling/interview language; asked face-to-face it sounds blunt, like 'State your occupation.' Seoul speakers ask 무슨 일 해요? (politer still: 무슨 일 하세요?). 하다 is engine-derivable, stays 해요체 present.

fix.english: What do you do for work?
fix.grammar: 무슨 일 해요? (museun il haeyo) — literally 'what work do you do?' — the natural way to ask a job.

issue: Self-honorific: 선생님 contains the honorific suffix -님, so 저는 선생님이에요 honors ONESELF — same violation class as attaching 씨 to one's own name (register policy rule 4). The humble job-title word is 교사. (Heard colloquially, but a strict register model shouldn't canonize it; NIKL flags it.)

fix.grammar: 교사 (gyosa) = teacher as a job title; 선생님 honors OTHERS — never use it for yourself.

issue: Policy rule 2 violation: 합니다체 form (감사합니다) modeled with NO tip naming the speech level — policy requires 'always with a tip naming the level.' ko-0043's tip does not attach to this card. Sentence itself is natural; fix adds the required tip only.

fix.grammar: 감사합니다 (gamsahamnida) is formal 합니다체 (hamnida-che) — thanks to strangers stays formal.

issue: Stilted pairing: 저기요 (attention-getter) + bare 죄송해요 (apology) don't combine in real speech. Hailing someone you'd follow with a request (죄송한데요…); squeezing past you'd say 잠시만요. As modeled it reads as an English 'Excuse me, sorry' calque.

fix.grammar: 저기요 (jeogiyo) hails a stranger or waiter; 잠시만요 (jamsimanyo) = 'just a moment, please.'

issue: Missing subject honorific: an adult describing their own father's actions uses -시- (아버지는 신문을 보세요); plain 봐요 about one's father sounds childish/rude to natives. Engine can't derive 보세요 (would give 보셔요), so the safe in-constraint fix swaps to a junior family member — 동생 takes plain form and keeps the family tag and the 봐요-reading tip intact.

fix.english: My younger sibling reads the newspaper.
fix.grammar: 봐요 covers watching and casual reading: 신문을 봐요 (sinmun-eul bwayo = I read the paper).

issue: Missing subject honorific: 어머니는 요리를 좋아해요 — plain 좋아해요 about one's own mother; natives say 좋아하세요. Engine can't derive -세요 forms, so swap to a sibling: older siblings take optional/no -시- in modern speech, so 언니 + plain form is fully natural and keeps the family tag.

fix.grammar: 언니 (eonni) = a woman's older sister; men say 누나 (nuna).

언니.en: older sister (used by a female speaker)
